replacement.angle: How do you register a caching decorator around IProductRepository with the built-in Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection container and no third-party library?
replacement.answerHinge: The built-in container has no decorate API, so you register the concrete inner type and register the interface with a factory that resolves the inner type and wraps it in the decorator; registering both against the interface makes the decorator resolve itself or be ignored.

findings.reason: Both stubs hinge on keyed services (AddKeyed* plus FromKeyedServices) selecting an implementation by key; DI belongs to aspnet-core, whose Covers line names DI.

replacement.angle: Why do the .NET design guidelines suggest sealing classes that were not designed for extension, and what does sealing or unsealing later mean for consumers?
replacement.answerHinge: A class open to inheritance exposes its internal call sequence as a contract that derived classes rely on, so types not designed for extension are sealed; unsealing later is a compatible change while sealing an existing public class breaks derived types.

findings.reason: Both hinge on the anemic model judgement: entities with only getters and setters and rules in a service let any code bypass invariants; the anemic domain model is a DDD subject owned by architecture.

replacement.angle: During a major outage five engineers debug in one chat channel, nobody updates stakeholders and two people roll back conflicting changes; what do you do?
replacement.answerHinge: Declare an incident with explicit roles - an incident commander who coordinates and decides, an operations lead who changes the system and a communications lead who updates stakeholders - so coordination is separated from fixing and only agreed changes are made.

findings.reason: Both hinge on the same judgement that pages must be urgent, actionable and symptom-based, with noisy alerts removed or downgraded; alert quality is observability owned by devops.

replacement.angle: A platform team wants every cloud service (queues, storage, secrets) wrapped behind Abstract Factory and Adapter layers so all services stay portable between clouds; what are the long-term trade-offs?
replacement.answerHinge: A blanket portability layer forces the lowest common denominator of the providers, leaks provider semantics anyway and must be maintained by the platform team, so abstraction is applied only where switching providers is a real requirement and elsewhere a thin adapter at the service edge is enough.

findings.reason: Both stubs hinge on the same judgement that mandatory company-wide base classes (BaseService, BaseController) couple all services through the fragile base class and should be replaced by composition; inheritance versus composition is owned by oop-solid.

replacement.angle: Select the true statements about Counter, UpDownCounter and the observable instruments in System.Diagnostics.Metrics.
replacement.answerHinge: A Counter only increases and fits totals such as handled requests, an UpDownCounter can also decrease and fits values such as items in a queue, and observable instruments report through a callback that runs only when a listener collects, not on every change.

findings.reason: Both multi stubs hinge on which schema changes are safe while the previous app version runs against the migrated database (additive yes, rename, drop or NOT NULL no); migrations are owned by ef-core.

replacement.angle: The product page calls a recommendation service synchronously, and whenever that service slows down the whole page becomes slow; what do you change?
replacement.answerHinge: An optional dependency on the critical path must not decide the page latency, so its call gets a short timeout and a circuit breaker and the page renders without recommendations or with a cached fallback when it fails.

findings.reason: Both hinge on the same judgement that a health probe failing on a shared dependency takes every healthy instance out at once, so the probe must check only the process itself; cloud-containers-12 covers it concretely for Kubernetes probes.

replacement.angle: Across a fleet of .NET worker services, should an unexpected exception in a background loop be caught and the loop continued, or should the process crash, and what must the platform provide for that choice?
replacement.answerHinge: After an unexpected exception the process state may be inconsistent, so the default since .NET 6 is that an unhandled BackgroundService exception stops the host, and letting it crash is safe only when an orchestrator restarts it and the work is idempotent and resumable, while catch-all loops keep broken processes alive silently.

findings.reason: Both hinge on translating failures into a stable RFC 9457 Problem Details contract with error codes instead of exposing internals; the error contract of HTTP APIs is owned by web-api.

replacement.angle: What team rules do you set for requesting runtime permissions such as location or camera in a MAUI app so the behaviour is consistent across Android and iOS?
replacement.answerHinge: Permissions are checked with Permissions.CheckStatusAsync and requested with RequestAsync at the point of use on the main thread, behind one shared service that also handles the denied state with an explanation, because each platform declares permissions differently and a denied request may not show the prompt again.

findings.reason: maui-24 hinges on the same judgement as maui-11: keep platform code in Platforms folders or partial classes behind one shared API instead of scattered #if blocks.

replacement.angle: A team plans to persist records for years by writing struct memory directly to files with MemoryMarshal.AsBytes; which statement about this design is correct?
replacement.answerHinge: Raw struct bytes depend on field layout, padding and the platform's byte order, so a durable format must be written field by field with an explicit endianness, for example with BinaryPrimitives, and carry a version.

findings.reason: Both architect single stubs hinge on the same fact: millions of small managed objects make full GC marking expensive, and an array of reference-free structs fixes it; the GC pause root cause is owned by clr-gc.
